When sensor data fail,
irrigation decisions
can go wrong.
Research evidence, prototype design and validation roadmap
Evidence-led design for an uncertainty-aware irrigation twin
Sources: supplied papers and project prototype documentation.
A faulty reading can reverse the right irrigation decision
A sensor may report a dry field when soil is saturated—or hide a real moisture deficit.
Unneeded irrigation wastes water and may increase crop or disease risk.
A confident point forecast can hide missing, drifting or out-of-range inputs.
Need: estimate the field state, show uncertainty, then gate action.
Problem framing synthesizes the supplied smart-irrigation review and prototype README, which discuss sensor dropout, drift and data quality.
Paper 1 | Can soil-carbon predictions show when they may be wrong?
Test whether conformal prediction can make ML estimates of soil organic carbon (SOC) more reliable for end users.
2015 LUCAS topsoil samples (0–20 cm) across Europe; SOC ranged from 0.1 to 560.2 g/kg.
28 covariates: TerraClimate, Landsat-8 bands / indices, and terrain variables.
Conformalized Quantile Random Forest (CQRF), compared with bootstrap RF, quantile boosting, quantile neural network and quantile linear regression.
Conformal scores adjust the RF quantiles
α is the target miscoverage rate: 10% nominally means 90% of true values should fall inside intervals.

Source: Kakhani, N. et al. (2024), “Uncertainty Quantification of Soil Organic Carbon Estimation from Remote Sensing Data with Conformal Prediction,” Remote Sensing 16(3), 438. https://doi.org/10.3390/rs16030438.

title: RESEARCH PAPER 1 • RESULTS AND PROJECT GAP

text: RESEARCH PAPER 1 • RESULTS AND PROJECT GAP
Paper 1 | Calibrated intervals covered more cases—but were wider
Held-out mean results across five test seeds
PICP = % of observed SOC values inside intervals (target 90%). PINAW = interval width normalized by data range; lower is narrower.
MAE = average absolute prediction error. RMSE = square root of average squared error, so large misses count more. Both errors are in g/kg SOC; lower is better.
CQRF reached 90% coverage with the narrowest intervals among strong-coverage methods. Bootstrap RF had lower MAE/RMSE, but covered only 25% of test values.

Gap this solution targets: static European SOC mapping does not handle in-season moisture forecasts, faulty telemetry or action gating. AgriTwin extends uncertainty-aware decisions to irrigation; it remains a prototype pending field validation.

Source: Kakhani et al. (2024), Table 4. PICP is prediction interval coverage probability; PINAW is prediction interval normalized average width; MAE is mean absolute error; RMSE is root mean square error. Results are from European SOC estimation and do not validate irrigation use. https://doi.org/10.3390/rs16030438.
Paper 2 | Which model best predicts soil moisture across depth and time?
Wang et al. (2024) · Hydrology and Earth System Sciences
Compare machine-learning and deep-learning structures for soil-moisture forecasting across sites, soil depths and lead times.
30 ISMN sites; five depths (0.05–1.0 m). Inputs include precipitation, air temperature, long- and shortwave radiation, wind, humidity, soil temperature and prior moisture.
3 ML baselines (RF, ELM, SVR) plus 10 deep models: CNN, LSTM, Transformer, hybrids, attention-LSTM variants and GAN-LSTM.
Four-day input history; forecast 1, 3 and 7 days. Time-ordered 6:2:2 train / validation / test split; 25 repeated training runs.
Metrics: R² measures variance captured (1 is perfect; 0 matches a mean baseline). RMSE is the root-mean-square forecast error; it penalizes large misses and uses the moisture data’s units.
Source: Wang, Y. et al. (2024), “A comprehensive study of deep learning for soil moisture prediction,” Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 28, 917–943. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-28-917-2024.

title: RESEARCH PAPER 2 • RESULTS AND PROJECT GAP

text: RESEARCH PAPER 2 • RESULTS AND PROJECT GAP
Paper 2 | Feature attention improved skill; horizon still mattered
R² ranges from 0 to 1 in the positive range: higher means more observed variation is captured; a negative value means worse than predicting the mean.
FA-LSTM ranked ahead of temporal-attention variants in most cases; gains were also seen at deeper layers.
GAN-LSTM outperformed standard LSTM in most settings, especially at 3–7 days, with similar computational cost.
LSTM was a strong baseline; accuracy varied by site, depth and forecast horizon.

Gap this solution targets: forecasts alone do not quantify decision confidence or test safe irrigation actions during sensor faults and pathogen risk. AgriTwin adds an uncertainty band and explicit safety gates; these additions need real-data validation.
RMSE = square root of mean squared forecast error; lower is better, and large errors weigh more heavily.

Source: Wang et al. (2024), Table 5 and Sections 4.1, 4.4, 4.5. FA-LSTM R² values at 0.20 m are 0.965 (1 day), 0.925 (3 days) and 0.849 (7 days), for the 10-site subset. Authors report FA-LSTM best among attention variants in most situations and GAN-LSTM outperforming LSTM in most scenarios. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-28-917-2024.
Review | What data and methods are converging in smart irrigation?
Aim: synthesize how ML and digital twins combine for irrigation scheduling, simulation and control.
Structured review of 2019–2024 literature; searches included Scopus, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore and Google Scholar.
A literature synthesis, not a new field experiment.

Source: Bautista, C. J. C., Gallegos, R. K. B., & Lampayan, R. M., “Machine learning and digital twins in smart irrigation: optimising water use through agricultural data analytics,” Digital Twin 3(1), Article 2562418. Published online 12 Nov 2025. https://doi.org/10.1080/27525783.2025.2562418.

title: RESEARCH REVIEW • FINDINGS AND OPEN CHALLENGES

text: RESEARCH REVIEW • FINDINGS AND OPEN CHALLENGES
Review | A twin joins sensing, prediction, simulation and action
ML forecasts plus simulation can test schedules before action.
Noisy / missing sensors; mismatched data; weak rural networks; site-specific models; limited interpretability.
Many examples are pilots; cost, interoperability and grower workflow still constrain deployment.
Project relevance: AgriTwin prototypes uncertainty-aware control and simulated fault testing; it does not yet resolve field validation or adoption barriers.
Source: Bautista et al. (2025/2026), system integration, limitations and future directions. The stages shown synthesize the review architecture.
Other teams are building field-linked crop and irrigation twins
Low-cost IoT and deep models infer crop and environment states with day-to-day updates.
Planned evaluation through a soybean growth season on a real research farm.
Combines soil-moisture IoT, satellite observations and ground-penetrating radar for irrigation.
Reported twin implementation with Ivars and Bell-lloc cooperatives.
Combines crop-growth and logistics models with camera-based crop status.
Validation uses historical and current TOM4.0 crop cycles.
Shared direction: fuse sensors with models, update the virtual state, and test against operating conditions.

Sources: CropTwin, University of Nebraska–Lincoln (https://int-lab.unl.edu/croptwin/); AI4WATER, UPC (https://agrotech.upc.edu/en/projects-events/ai4water/view); DigiTom, EU CAP Network (https://eu-cap-network.ec.europa.eu/projects/practice-abstracts/digitom_en). Project evidence stages are stated as described by each page; they are not directly comparable.

Future work | Move from a credible demo to a field-tested twin
Connect in-situ soil moisture and crop-stage observations; measure sensor drift, packet loss and time mismatch.
Test forecast skill, interval coverage, pathogen rules and dry limits across soils, cultivars and horizons.
Compare recommendations with grower practice; log water, energy, crop outcomes and overrides before valve automation.
Improve interoperability and low-connectivity operation; evaluate edge deployment after safety evidence.
Scale-up gate: verified uncertainty behavior + safe, human-supervised outcomes.
